opus-5.5.text:
I think the first instinct for a lot of researchers who become founders is to go big right away: a huge vision, a huge team, a huge compute budget. I understand why. In AI right now it feels like the only thing that matters is scale. But for a first undertaking, I'd choose something deliberately smaller than my ambition and larger than my comfort zone.

The way I think about it, the first project has two jobs. One is to produce something real that people actually use. The other, maybe more important, is to teach you how to be a founder: hiring, making decisions with incomplete information, saying no to things. If the scope is too large, you never get feedback. You spend two years building and you don't know whether you were right or wrong. If it's too small, you learn the mechanics, but you don't learn anything about the hard problem you actually care about.

So the scale I'd pick is one where, within six months to a year, you can get a clear signal. Either the core technical bet works or it doesn't, and either users care or they don't. And it should sit on a path toward the bigger thing. It shouldn't be a detour. Ideally, the first product is a piece of the long-term vision that can stand on its own.

Team size works the same way. A small, very dense team, where everyone understands the whole system, beats a big team in the early phase. Coordination cost grows faster than people realize, and in research-heavy work, a few people with very high context can move remarkably fast.

So my short answer is: start with the smallest scope that still forces you to confront the real question. Earn the right to scale through the signal you get, not through the size of the story you tell at the beginning.

r001.rationale: It recommends starting with the smallest scope that still addresses the real question, and says the first product should be part of a larger vision and sit on a path toward the bigger goal.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that I wouldn't start by choosing a scale at all. I'd start by choosing a problem, and the scale sort of falls out of that.

When I was doing research, the mistake I saw most often, and made myself, was deciding "I want to do something big" or "I want to do something small and safe" before actually understanding what the thing was. The ReAct paper, for example, was a tiny project. It was a few weeks, a simple idea: let the model think and act in the same loop. It wasn't scoped to be important. It became important because the underlying question, how do you let a language model interact with an environment, turned out to be the right question at the right time. If I had tried to "scale" it up front, build the big agent platform, I probably would have gotten lost in infrastructure and missed the core insight.

So for a first undertaking as a founder, the frame I'd use is: what is the smallest thing I can build that tests whether my belief about the world is true? Not the smallest thing that's a product, the smallest thing that's an experiment. If you believe agents are going to do real work in some domain, you don't need a company-scale bet to find out. You need one environment, one task, one user who actually cares, and you need to see whether the thing works end to end.

The reason I'd keep it small isn't caution, it's speed of learning. Right now the field moves so fast that the cost of being wrong for a long time is enormous. A big first bet means you're committed to assumptions that might be obsolete in six months. A small bet means you can be wrong quickly, update, and try again. In some sense the right "scale" is whatever lets you run the most iterations before your information goes stale.

The one caveat is that the problem itself should be big, even if the first step is small. I'd be very reluctant to work on something where even total success is uninteresting. The ambition lives in the direction, not in the size of the first move. You pick a direction where, if you're right, the ceiling is very high, and then you take the smallest concrete step that teaches you whether you're actually right.

So, short version: pick a direction that matters, make the first step embarrassingly small, and measure yourself by how fast you learn rather than how big you look.

r001.rationale: The response recommends an initially small experiment and says to choose a direction with a high ceiling, so its potential extends beyond that first step.

astra-6.text:
我会选一个足够小、能很快验证，但又能通向更大问题的切入点。第一步不一定要做一个很大的产品，但你得想清楚：如果这一步做成了，它为什么值得继续往下做？

比如，你能不能先帮一类用户解决一个具体问题，让他们愿意持续使用，甚至愿意付钱？这个阶段最重要的是把假设变成反馈。你觉得技术很厉害，跟用户觉得这个东西有用，中间可能差得很远。

所以我会把长期的野心和短期的工作量分开。长期可以想得很大，短期最好是一个小团队在几个月里能验证的事情。做完之后，你应该更清楚用户需要什么、技术还缺什么，以及下一步值不值得投入。如果第一步就需要很多人、很多钱，几年以后才能知道方向对不对，我会比较谨慎。

r001.rationale: Recommends a small first step that can be validated quickly while leading toward a larger problem.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d separate the ambition from the scope of the first product. You can have a very ambitious view of where the world is going, but the first thing you build should be narrow enough that you can actually finish it, put it in people’s hands, and learn whether they care.

I’d look for a problem where I have some particular insight, where a small team can deliver something useful, and where solving it opens up a larger opportunity. If the initial undertaking requires a huge organization before you can test your core assumption, that would make me cautious. You’re committing a lot before you’ve learned very much.

But I wouldn’t choose something small just because it’s easy, either. The question is: if this works, what does it let us do next? Ideally, the first step is concrete and manageable, while the direction leaves room to build something much bigger.

r001.rationale: It recommends a concrete, manageable first step that can open a larger opportunity and lead to something much bigger.
